quote: Problem: Beweis, dass, wenn eine lineare [-ganzzahl-] Sub- stitution mit ganzzahligen Coefficienten gegeben ist, diese nur eine endliche Zahl von Invarianten (d.h. ganze ganzzahlige Funktion der n Variabeln) giebt, durch welche sich alle anderen ganzen ganzzahlig[?] Invarianten ganz und ganzzahlig ausdrücken lässt.
english: Problem: Proof that, when a linear substitution with integer coefficients is given, it has only a finite number of invariants (i.e. integral integer-coefficient functions of the n variables) by which all other integral integer-coefficient invariants can be expressed integrally and with integer coefficients.
topic: A list of research notes: upper bounds for the coefficients of the characteristic function following Noether, representations of a multiple of a ternary form as a sum of three squares, counting contact curves via Abelian functions, and finiteness of integral invariants of an integral linear substitution.

triage.modern_statement: Take g in GL_n(Z) (or any n×n integer matrix) acting linearly on Z[x_1,...,x_n]. Is the ring of invariants Z[x_1,...,x_n]^g = {f : f(gx) = f(x)} finitely generated as a Z-algebra? In other words, are there finitely many integer-coefficient invariant polynomials such that every other one is a polynomial in them with integer coefficients? This is the integral, single-matrix special case of the finite-generation question that later became Hilbert's 14th problem.
triage.answered_by: If g has finite order, the cyclic group G = <g> is finite, and Emmy Noether's 1926 finiteness theorem settles it: 'Der Endlichkeitssatz der Invarianten endlicher linearer Gruppen der Charakteristik p', Nachr. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen 1926, pp. 28–35. She proved that A^G is finitely generated for a finite group G. Her proof was stated over a field but extends directly to any Noetherian base ring, including Z, by way of Hilbert's basis theorem and integrality of A over A^G. If g has infinite order, the closest result I found is over a field of characteristic 0: Weitzenböck's 1932 theorem that the invariants of a single unipotent transformation form a finitely generated algebra. I found no source that explicitly handles a general infinite-order integer matrix over Z.

evidence.claim: Noether's 1926 paper on the finiteness of invariants of finite linear groups (Göttinger Nachrichten, pp. 28–35).

For finite groups, Hilbert's 14th problem was answered affirmatively by Noether in 1926 (A^G finitely generated). Her proof generalizes straightforwardly to a Noetherian coefficient ring R, using Hilbert's basis theorem and the fact that A is a finite module over the invariant subring.
In 1926 Noether proved that the ring of invariants of a modular representation of a finite group is finitely generated.
Weitzenböck's classical theorem says the algebra of invariants of a single unipotent transformation g in GL_m(K) acting on K[X] is finitely generated.
Hilbert's 14th problem (1900) asks whether certain invariant algebras are finitely generated. It is the general setting this note falls under.

triage.why: The note asks whether the integer invariants of one integer linear substitution have a finite integral basis. This is an early special case of the finite-generation problem in invariant theory, which Hilbert later posed in general as his 14th problem; the note itself is not one of the published problems. For a substitution of finite order (a finite cyclic group), Noether's 1926 theorem answers it positively, and a survey source says her argument extends to Noetherian base rings such as Z. For infinite order, I found a positive result only over a field (Weitzenböck 1932, unipotent case). My guess is that the general integral case follows from standard theory, but no source I found states this, so I have not counted it as established. Work on Hilbert's 14th problem and on Weitzenböck/unipotent invariants continues today, but I have no evidence that this exact integral question is being actively studied, so 'active_today' is 'unclear'.
